title: The sacrifice
hookLine: an animal is sacrificed, and the meat shared

cards: A rule about leftovers, and then a change to it. One Eid in Medina, Aisha reports, a group of poor families arrived from the desert.
The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told the people: keep the meat of your sacrifice for three days, and give away the rest. Later, people came to him unsure. Were they still bound by it?
His answer: I only forbade it because of the families who had come. Now eat, store, and give. The rule had been shaped around hungry guests.

teach.b: Back at Mina, after the stoning, Jabir's account in Sahih Muslim says the Prophet went to the place of sacrifice and offered animals with his own hand.
Then a piece from each was cooked, and he ate of the meat and drank of the broth. That's the first thing to notice: the one who offered it sat down and ate. The sacrifice becomes a meal.

teach.h: THE CONTENT AND THE ONE WHO ASKS.
teach.b: Surah Al-Hajj tells those who sacrifice to eat of it and to feed two kinds of people: the one who is content and doesn't ask, and the one who does ask. The quiet poor, and the poor who knock.
Third, the line that turns the whole act around.
The same surah says: "Their flesh and their blood reach not Allah, but the devotion from you reacheth Him." The meat stays here, on plates. What goes up is something you can't weigh.

teach.h: A RULE SHAPED BY HUNGRY GUESTS.
teach.b: Fourth, Aisha's story from the hook, in Sahih Muslim: a rule about storing meat, set because hungry families had come, and loosened when they hadn't. The sacrifice keeps looking at who is at the door.
And it isn't only for pilgrims. At Eid al-Adha, Muslims at home who are able offer an animal too, and remember Ibrahim, whose story of a ransomed son is told in Surah As-Saffat.

teach.h: THEIR FLESH AND THEIR BLOOD REACH NOT ALLAH.
teach.b: So the same day, at Mina and far from it, there's blood, then a fire, then a pot, then a knock, then a plate passed across a table.

how: Pilgrims offer an animal at Mina after the stoning, and Muslims at home who are able offer one at Eid al-Adha; the meat is eaten by the household and shared with friends and with people in need.

o: an animal offered for God, its meat eaten and shared
the money pilgrims pay to make the journey
giving up a favorite food for the days of Hajj

p: he ate of the meat and drank the broth
feed the content and the one who asks
the rule shaped by hungry families

s: the Qur'an says the flesh and blood of the sacrifice reach God
it says the reverse: their flesh and blood reach not Allah, but the devotion does.
the Prophet once limited storing the meat because hungry families had arrived
Aisha reports it, and later he said: now eat, store, and give.
the meat is only for people who ask for it
Surah Al-Hajj names the content who don't ask, and those who do.

games.q: some time after the rule about storing meat. you ask the Prophet whether you still have to give away whatever is left after three days. what does he say?
o: it was because of the hungry families. now eat, store, and give.
games.why: he explains the rule was for the families who had come, and loosens it: eat, store, and give in charity.

practice: Think of the food you'll eat in the next day or two, and of one person who could share some of it: someone who'd never ask, a neighbor, an older relative, a coworker eating alone, or someone who would ask if they knew they could.
Picture handing them the plate. If you pray, thank God for the food first; if not, just hold the picture.

wordCard.voice: The sacrifice. An animal offered in God's name on the day of sacrifice, its meat eaten and shared, and only the devotion reaching God. Today's word.

orig.note: the pilgrim's offering at Mina; at home, the Eid sacrifice is called udhiyah.

carryVoice: Your line: shared meat. The week ran from Zamzam, through Safa and Marwa, Mina, Arafah and Muzdalifah, to the stones and the sacrifice. Eat well, and see you tomorrow.

sources.q: Their flesh and their blood reach not Allah, but the devotion from you reacheth Him.
